edges.description: Loss of amplification raises auditory thresholds in the affected band.
Acoustic overexposure is the trigger that turns the raised shear on the still-coupled outer hair cells into actual cell death.

Reproduces the ZP-domain structural lesion and elevated thresholds, and confirms that ZP and ZA variants damage the matrix differently. It does not reproduce human progression, and it shows a phenotype humans do not have.
edges.limitations: Thresholds are elevated across 8-40 kHz rather than in a mid-frequency band, and the mouse cochlea's frequency map differs from the human one, so the audiogram shape that defines the human disease cannot be modelled directly. The mice also develop audiogenic seizures, which is not a feature of human DFNA8/12.

edges.description: Reproduces the ZA-domain structural lesion and threshold elevation, but the phenotype is stable where the human one progresses.
edges.limitations: The human C1619S family has progressive high-frequency loss; the mouse carrying the same substitution does not deteriorate over the period studied, in either tectorial membrane structure or auditory function. Any study of progression, or of an intervention aimed at slowing it, cannot use this model as its readout.

edges.description: Shows partial uncoupling, raised shear on the still-coupled row, increased prestin-driven reticular lamina movement, greater noise vulnerability and excess outer hair cell death.
edges.limitations: The corresponding human phenotype is described as worsening over time, but the mouse's emission thresholds were stable to six months in quiet and the excess cell death was elicited by experimental noise exposure. The model therefore demonstrates a vulnerability rather than spontaneous progression, and the noise exposure has no defined human equivalent.

nodes.description: Bilateral, usually symmetric sensorineural loss, most often prelingual and frequently U-shaped on the audiogram with the maximum around 2 kHz. Whether it stays put or worsens, and which frequencies it takes, is partly predicted by the mutated domain. Vestibular function is spared and there are no extra-auditory features — this is a nonsyndromic deafness.

evidence.reference_title: Autosomal-dominant, prelingual, nonprogressive sensorineural hearing loss: localization of the gene (DFNA8) to chromosome 11q by linkage in an Austrian family.
evidence.snippet: The hearing loss was moderate to severe, a pure tone audiogram showing a U-shaped form with maximum loss at 2, 000 Hz.

nodes.description: Active amplification by the outer hair cells is lost or degraded in the affected frequency band. In the alpha-tectorin null mouse, where the membrane is detached and stripped of non-collagenous matrix, the basilar membrane is still tuned but 35 dB less sensitive, and the second resonance that reveals the membrane acting as an inertial mass disappears. The organ of Corti is otherwise architecturally normal, which is what makes this an amplification failure rather than a sensory-cell disease.

nodes.description: For severe-to-profound loss, or where amplification stops being enough. Outcomes in TECTA-related loss are good, which follows from the lesion being an extracellular mechanical one: an implant bypasses the failed tectorial membrane coupling entirely and stimulates a hair-cell and neural apparatus that is structurally intact. Electric-acoustic stimulation is the relevant variant where low-frequency residual hearing is preserved, as it often is in the mid-frequency-loss configurations.

evidence.reference_title: Massively parallel DNA sequencing successfully identifies new causative mutations in deafness genes in patients with cochlear implantation and EAS.
evidence.snippet: Satisfactory auditory performance after receiving a CI/EAS in patients with certain deafness gene mutations indicates that genetic testing would be helpful in predicting CI/EAS outcomes and deciding treatment choices.

nodes.description: The tectorial membrane is built in the endolymph from type II collagen fibrils crosslinked by alpha- and beta-tectorin, adhering medially to the spiral limbus through a tectorin-rich matrix on the interdental cell membranes and contacting outer hair cell stereocilia at its lower surface. Mutant alpha-tectorin disturbs this assembly, and — the point that makes the genotype-phenotype correlation mechanistic rather than statistical — the ZP and ZA domains do so in structurally distinct ways, shown directly in mice carrying the human alleles.

nodes.description: Not a cause of the disease, but the exposure that converts its structural lesion into progressive cell loss. Because a shortened or abnormal tectorial membrane concentrates shear on the outer hair cells still coupled to it, the same acoustic insult that a normal cochlea recovers from is not fully recovered from here. This is the mechanistic reason noise protection is advised in TECTA-related hearing loss rather than a general precaution.

nodes.description:
A conserved residue is replaced in one of the modular domains of alpha-tectorin — entactin/NIDO, the von Willebrand factor type D / zonadhesin repeats, or the C-terminal zona pellucida domain. A recurring subclass substitutes or introduces a cysteine, which matters because the matrix is held together partly by disulfide crosslinks. Unbiased screening of a Spanish and an American cohort found variants in every domain of the protein, including the entactin domain and the vWFD1-3 repeats.
Not every dominant allele is a simple missense change. A separate class of coding variants acts by altering RNA splicing, producing in-frame deletions rather than a substituted residue — c.5999G>A (p.Gly2000Glu) causes aberrant splicing of exon 20, and c.5383+6T>A skips exon 16. These matter twice over: they are missed if splicing effects of coding variants are not examined, and they carry the most direct evidence that the mechanism is not haploinsufficiency, since carrier transcript levels are unchanged.

nodes.description: The membrane's job is to deliver shear to the outer hair cell bundles and to provide an inertial mass for them to push against. When it is shortened it contacts only the first row of outer hair cells, leaving the rest uncoupled and — by computational estimate — raising shear force on the row that remains attached by about half. That is a mechanical explanation for why a partial structural defect both reduces hearing and endangers the surviving coupled cells.

nodes.description: A slower, secondary process rather than the primary lesion. Because uncoupling concentrates shear on the outer hair cells that remain attached, and because prestin expression rises in the mutant, those cells are more easily damaged — mutant mice recover incompletely from a noise exposure that wild-type mice recover from fully, and lose outer hair cells preferentially from the first row. This is the best available mechanistic account of why some genotypes progress, though it has not been demonstrated in human temporal bones.
